selectedEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.

selectedEvidence.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

selectedEvidence.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
selectedEvidence.name: Rhetoric in Action
selectedEvidence.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.

selectedEvidence.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
selectedEvidence.name: Persuasive Communication
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.

selectedEvidence.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
selectedEvidence.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

selectedEvidence.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
selectedEvidence.name: African Art & Heritage
selectedEvidence.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
selectedEvidence.discipline: African art history; Cultural heritage studies; Museum studies
selectedEvidence.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
selectedEvidence.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research

selectedEvidence.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
selectedEvidence.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.

selectedEvidence.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
selectedEvidence.name: Writing Art's Histories

selectedEvidence.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
selectedEvidence.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
selectedEvidence.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.

selectedEvidence.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

selectedEvidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
selectedEvidence.name: Great Literary Works
selectedEvidence.profile: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.

selectedEvidence.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
selectedEvidence.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

selectedEvidence.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
selectedEvidence.name: World Myth & Literature
selectedEvidence.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.

selectedEvidence.description2: Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.
selectedEvidence.name: Life & Travel Writing
selectedEvidence.profile: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.

selectedEvidence.description2: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
selectedEvidence.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning

selectedEvidence.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
selectedEvidence.name: Introduction to Film & Media
selectedEvidence.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.

selectedEvidence.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
selectedEvidence.name: Media Archaeology
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.

selectedEvidence.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
selectedEvidence.name: Media & Race
selectedEvidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.

selectedEvidence.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
selectedEvidence.name: The Documentary
selectedEvidence.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.

selectedEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
selectedEvidence.name: Ethics

Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. schedules.label: International politics, political economy & regional change
schedules.concept: The closest feasible UCR response integrates international-relations theory, comparative and EU politics, political economy, law, global and imperial history, sociology, cultural analysis, communication and quantitative and qualitative research. It examines how global political and economic change affects regions and local societies without claiming the comparator’s Arabic-language or Africa-specialist sequence.
schedules.labelReason: The completed curriculum balances politics, political economy, history, sociology, law and cultural analysis. The label reflects that broad international-studies composition and does not imply Arabic proficiency or Africa-area expertise.
progression: Current offerings and formal prerequisites checked for all placements. Law and statistics gateways precede their dependent courses; at least six 300-level courses, four per term, 24 unique selections and Year-1 PPD. Retained foundation-before-advanced sequencing where feasible; no invented formal prerequisites. Machine Learning has no formal prerequisite; statistical preparation is supplied earlier.

schedules.label: Global cultures, communication & historical inquiry
schedules.concept: Studies how literature, media, heritage and communication shape identity and interpretations of the past. Comparative imperial history, African art, American cultural history and historical inquiry connect cultural expression to power and colonial legacies. Stylistics, ethics, philosophy of emotion, rhetoric, qualitative methods and advanced literary and art-historical interpretation provide different ways to investigate meaning. It does not supply a foreign-language sequence or comprehensive regional specialisation.
schedules.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by history, literature, media, communication, heritage and sociocultural research. The label states that emphasis while avoiding a claim to Arabic-language or comprehensive regional-area training.
progression: Current offerings and formal prerequisites checked for all placements. Law and statistics gateways precede their dependent courses; at least six 300-level courses, four per term, 24 unique selections and Year-1 PPD. schedules.distinctness: The cultural-history route differs from the closest response by 13 courses / 97.5 EC in each direction. It replaces most economics, politics and governance study with literature, media, language, heritage and advanced humanities research; the difference follows directly from its cultural and regional-history concept.

schedules.label: International politics, conflict & global justice
schedules.concept: A third defensible route concentrating on international order and the institutions used to govern conflict and injustice. It combines international relations, public international and EU law, human rights, comparative constitutional systems, political economy, security history, peace and conflict, radicalisation, data analysis and qualitative and historical research.
schedules.labelReason: The completed curriculum has a clear concentration in politics, law, conflict, justice and evidence-based governance. The label reflects that concentration without claiming diplomacy training or a regional-language specialisation.
progression: Current offerings and formal prerequisites checked for all placements. schedules.distinctness: The conflict-and-justice route differs from the closest response by 10 courses / 75 EC and from the cultural-history route by 19 courses / 142.5 EC in each direction. Its law, security, radicalisation and data-analysis sequence is a substantive third organising choice.
